Perched amid Rio de Janeiro’s urban sprawl and rolling hills, the Maracanã Stadium’s vast white canopy glows under evening lights. Since its hurried inauguration in June 1950 for the World Cup, the arena has witnessed two World Cup finals, legendary football matches, and performances by global music stars. It has also hosted Pope John Paul II, Queen Elizabeth II, and annual Santa Claus landings that drew massive crowds.

Decades of renovations—most notably for the 2007 Pan American Games and the 2014 World Cup—have modernized seating, lighting, and video screens, though some long-time fans lament the loss of the old general admission terraces. Now managed by the Fla-Flu consortium, Maracanã welcomes hundreds of thousands of visitors each year through stadium tours and events. Upcoming enhancements include upgraded field illumination, new screens, and the planned Football Museum opening in 2027.

The Maracanã stadium, officially known as Estádio Jornalista Mário Filho, stands as a legendary sports venue in Brazil’s largest city. Opened in 1950 to host the FIFA World Cup final, it famously accommodated a record crowd of 199,854 spectators. Over the decades, it has undergone several renovations, reducing its capacity to 78,838 seats while modernizing facilities and ensuring safety standards.

From this aerial vantage point, the stadium’s circular bowl and expansive roof structure dominate the surrounding urban fabric of Rio de Janeiro. The venue continues to host top-tier football matches, concerts, and cultural events, maintaining its status as a symbol of Brazilian sporting heritage.

A state-of-the-art ring-cable structure now supports the Maracanã Stadium’s new PTFE-glass-fiber membrane roof. Sixty radial steel cables connect three inner tension rings to an outer compression ring composed of 60 steel segments. These segments rest on movable supports to absorb thermal expansion, and the entire assembly was lifted into place using a synchronized “Big Lift” procedure. The membrane spans 68 meters from the outer ring to the central 160×122 meter opening, with valleys between cable layers channeling rainwater toward the inner opening or outer ring.

Beneath the roof, the seating bowl was reconfigured with steeper, more compact stands, increasing capacity to 78,800 spectators. The historic exterior façade remains preserved under heritage protection, while the widened outer ring carries photovoltaic panels as a symbolic gesture toward sustainable energy. Alpine workers completed the membrane installation at 30 meters above the pitch, ensuring a lightweight, UV-stable cover that blends engineering innovation with architectural heritage.

A central compression ring and three tension rings form a horizontal spoked‐wheel system, with high‐strength cables radiating outward to support a PTFE‐coated fiberglass membrane. This diagram presents the eight sequential phases for erecting the steel roof over Arena Grêmio’s seating bowl. Each phase—labeled from 1 to 8—covers a specific sector: North, East, Northeast, South, Southeast, West, Southwest, and Northwest. The color‑coded overlay aligns with the stadium’s rounded‑corner rectangular footprint, showing where trussed cantilevers and bracing systems will be installed in each stage.

The roof spans 42,400 m² above 60,540 seats, supported by 96 trussed cantilevers fixed to existing concrete stands. Horizontal and vertical bracing rings ensure load transfer and compatibility of deformations between more flexible and stiffer trusses. Wind‑tunnel tests by LAC/UFRGS defined pressure coefficients up to 1.55 (uplift) and 0.70 (downforce), guiding design per Brazilian NBR standards and Eurocodes. Phased assembly allows each sector to resist environmental loads independently, addressing transport constraints and tight construction schedules.

O infográfico detalha o histórico de atrasos e estouros de orçamento na construção do Estádio Olímpico João Havelange, o Engenhão, desde o anúncio em janeiro de 2003 até a previsão de testes para a Olimpíada de 2016. Inicialmente orçado em R$ 60 milhões, o custo subiu para R$ 380 milhões, com sucessivos adiamentos de entrega entre 2004 e 2007. Após a inauguração em junho de 2007, o Botafogo assumiu a gestão, mas em março de 2010 já surgiram alertas sobre falhas na cobertura.

Em março de 2013, um laudo da empresa alemã RBS apontou risco de colapso dos arcos leste e oeste em ventos acima de 63 km/h, levando à interdição do estádio até o fim de 2014. O problema estrutural consistia em uma deformação 50% maior do que o previsto nos tubos dos arcos. A solução técnica envolve envolver esses tubos com uma capa de reforço e instalar colunas provisórias para garantir a estabilidade até a conclusão dos reparos, estimada para dezembro de 2014, com eventos-teste programados para 2015.
